source: Ordinary income brackets, standard deduction and long-term capital gains limits checked on 2026-10-07 against IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 as quoted in IRS pages and search extracts (the PDF itself was not opened); Roth IRA ranges from IRS Notice 2025-67 as quoted; the 415(c) total-additions limit (72000) from Notice 2025-67; the HSA limits from Rev. Proc. 2025-19 (not opened; the hsa_contributions section names its page in check_at); and the irmaa, qcd, senior_deduction and charitable_non_itemizer sections from several secondary sources that agree (each names its primary page in check_at); the other sections are 2026 estimates carried over from the model and an old config file (since removed), to check against SSA and CMS 2026 announcements

itemized_deductions.note: The SALT cap under P.L. 119-21 s.70120 (IRC 164(b)(7)): 40,000 in 2025, 40,400 in 2026, then 101% of the year before through 2029 (40,804.00 in 2027, 41,212.04 in 2028, 41,624.16 in 2029, compounded without rounding; practitioner tables round to whole dollars), with the phase-down threshold (505,000 in 2026) growing the same way; 30% of the modified AGI above the threshold is lost, never below 10,000. From 2030 the cap reverts to 10,000 (5,000 separate) with no phase-down. These are statute dollars, not indexed to inflation. Confirmed by secondary sources (NCSU farm law, TurboTax); the statute text was not read. The other itemized-deduction limits come from an old config file and are unconfirmed.

hsa_contributions.note: HSA contribution limits for 2026 from Rev. Proc. 2025-19 (self-only 4400, family 8750; the PDF was not opened). The catch-up from age 55 is set by statute and not indexed, so it is legislated (catch_up_adjustment): it follows the run's federal catch-up schedule while the limits follow inflation. hdhp_minimum_deductible is the lowest deductible a high-deductible health plan may have for an HSA (2026: 1700 self-only, 3400 family, from the same Rev. Proc., unconfirmed); it is indexed like the limits.

irmaa.note: 2026 income-related monthly adjustments per person, over the standard Part B premium: each tier applies to modified AGI above its threshold (a figure equal to a threshold stays in the tier below), except the top tier, which applies at or above its threshold, using the AGI of two years before. The thresholds except the last are taken to be indexed; the last (500000 single, 750000 joint, 391000 separate) is not indexed until 2028 (recalled, unconfirmed): top_threshold_adjustment and top_threshold_indexed_from hold it at its nominal level through 2027 and index it from 2028, with no random catch-up. MFS is a separate filer who lived with the spouse.

qcd.note: Qualified charitable distribution limit per person for 2026 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32 as quoted). It counts toward the required minimum distribution but not toward a Roth conversion.

senior_deduction.note: Deduction per person aged 65 or older at the end of the year, tax years 2025 to 2028 (P.L. 119-21, IRC 151(d)(5)(C), Schedule 1-A, as quoted). It lowers taxable income, not AGI, for itemizers and non-itemizers alike. Each person's amount falls by the rate times the modified AGI above the threshold (not indexed), so a joint couple with both 65 or older has none left at 250,000. The per-person phase-out rests on secondary sources; the Schedule 1-A instructions were not read. Separate filers get none.

charitable_non_itemizer.note: Deduction for cash gifts to charity taken with the standard deduction, from 2026 (P.L. 119-21, as quoted); gifts of securities or property and gifts to a donor-advised fund do not count. It lowers taxable income, not AGI. Whether the limit is indexed and the separate-filer amount (1000 assumed) are unconfirmed.

dependent_care_fsa.note: Dependent care assistance exclusion (IRC 129) for care of a qualifying child under 13 (IRC 21(b)(1)(A)). The limit of 7500 (3750 married filing separately) for tax years after 2025, raised from 5000 and 2500 by P.L. 119-21, and that it is not indexed, are from memory and unconfirmed; check IRS Publication 15-B and the Form 2441 instructions. The exclusion is also limited to the lower-earning spouse's earned income.

home_sale_exclusion.note: Section 121 exclusion of the gain on the sale of a main home: up to 250000 (500000 married filing jointly, 250000 for each separate return) when the home was owned and used as the main home for 2 of the 5 years before the sale; not indexed. Confirmed against IRS Publication 523 on 2026-10-20. The model assumes the ownership and use test is met, except that a home bought during the run and sold fewer than min_years later gets no exclusion (the partial exclusion for a shorter stay, depreciation recapture and the net investment income tax are not modelled).

estate_tax.note: Federal estate tax at death: the basic exclusion amount per person (IRC 2010(c)(3)) is 15,000,000 for 2026 under P.L. 119-21 s.70106, indexed for inflation after 2026, and the top rate (IRC 2001(c)) is 40% on the taxable estate above it. A surviving spouse may use the unused exclusion (portability, IRC 2010(c)(4)); the after-tax final worth doubles the exclusion for a joint return only. Checked 2026-10-22 against Rev. Proc. 2025-32 summaries (KPMG TaxNewsFlash 2025-10; Bowditch 2025-10-28): 2026 exclusion 15,000,000 (2025: 13,990,000), top rate 40%; portability needs a timely Form 706. State estate and inheritance taxes are in each state file's estate_inheritance section; the state death tax deduction (IRC 2058) is not modelled.

early_withdrawal.note: The additional tax on early distributions from qualified plans and IRAs (IRC 72(t)): penalty_rate of the taxable part of a distribution taken before age penalty_free_age (59 1/2). The rule of 55 (72(t)(2)(A)(v)): no additional tax on a 401k distribution after separation from service in or after the year the person reaches separation_age. Recalled, not checked against the page. The model charges it on Traditional withdrawals (not on the Roth conversion or a QCD) and on the Roth amounts the Roth rules penalize; ages are whole years, so age 59 pays all year. Not modelled: SEPP (72(t)(2)(A)(iv)), disability, death, medical, first-home, education, birth or adoption and the other exceptions; the age-50 public safety rule.

roth_distributions.check_at: https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590b (IRC 408A(d), 72(t)(6); Treas. Reg. 1.408A-6; IRC 72(e)(8) and Treas. Reg. 1.402A-1 for a Roth 401k)
roth_distributions.note: A Roth distribution is qualified (no tax) from age 59 1/2 once five_year_years have passed since the first Roth funding year. A Roth IRA (all of one owner's Roth IRAs as one pool) pays out contributions first, then conversions oldest first, then earnings (408A(d)(4)); a conversion taken out within five_year_years of its year and before 59 1/2 pays the additional tax on its once-taxed amount (72(t)(6)); earnings taken out unqualified are ordinary income and, before 59 1/2, penalized. A Roth 401k payout is split pro-rata between basis and earnings (72(e)(8)). The model reads five tax years as whole years (free when the year minus the funding year is at least five). Recalled, not checked against the page. Not modelled: a ten percent layer for conversions into a Roth 401k, a clock per Roth 401k plan versus per IRA owner, contribution-year layers, rollovers between Roth kinds.

hsa_nonmedical.note: An HSA distribution not used for qualified medical costs is ordinary income, plus penalty_rate of it before age penalty_free_age (the additional tax ends at 65, death or disability). Recalled, not checked against the page. The model draws the HSA for other spending only as a last resort, after every other account. Not modelled: state treatment (CA and NJ tax HSA money differently).

nonqualified_529.note: The earnings part of a 529 distribution not used for qualified education is ordinary income, plus penalty_rate of that part (the share of earnings is one less the account's basis over its balance). Recalled, not checked against the page. The model draws a 529 for other spending only as a last resort, after every account but the HSA. Not modelled: the scholarship, death, disability and Roth-rollover exceptions; state recapture.

aca_premium_credit.check_at: https://aspe.hhs.gov/topics/poverty-economic-mobility/poverty-guidelines, IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-25 and 26 USC 36B; dependent coverage: https://www.healthcare.gov/young-adults/children-under-26/ and 42 USC 300gg-14
aca_premium_credit.note: Marketplace (ACA) premium tax credit, 2026 coverage: the enhanced credits expired after 2025, so the credit ends completely above 400% of the federal poverty level (cliff_multiple, from CRS R48290 as quoted in the 2026-10-19 tax policy audit). Coverage year Y uses the poverty guideline published in Y-1 (the 2025 contiguous-states guideline here). The guideline figures were read back from the audit's cliff figures (62,600 for one person, 84,600 for two) and the HHS page itself was not opened. The 2026 applicable percentages (2.10% to 9.96% of income) are deliberately not stored: the model does not charge the credit, it only warns where the cliff is. dependent_coverage_age: a plan that covers children must keep a child on it until the 26th birthday (ACA dependent coverage, 42 USC 300gg-14); the model keeps each child on the household medical plan from birth until 26, whatever the child's spending years.

social_security_benefit_formula.note: Figures for estimating a retirement benefit from the earnings record, read from the SSA pages in check_at on 2026-10-12: the national average wage index for every year from 1951 to the newest published (a new year is added each October; the one historical series in the law files), the 2026 PIA bend points and the 90%, 32% and 15% factors (PIA rounded down to the dime), full retirement age in months by birth year (born_from is the first birth year of each row; a person born on January 1 counts in the previous year), the early-claim reduction (5/9 of 1% a month for the first 36 months early, 5/12 of 1% after) and the delayed-retirement credit for birth years 1943 and later (2/3 of 1% a month, to age 70). The 35 highest years count, divided by 420 months. A benefit can be claimed from min_claim_age (62) to max_claim_age (70); min_earning_years (10) years with earnings stand in for the 40 work credits a benefit needs (an approximation: four credits a year).
